name: Ivy Green
lede: Ivy green is a dark, muted olive green named for the leaves of ivy, and it is a surprisingly common color in painting.

sections.title: What the name means
sections.body:
Paterson's dictionary defines *ivy green* as a dark olive green [1]. The swatch here is a dull, greyish olive, and the nearest ISCC-NBS name is grayish olive green [2]. Ridgway's 1912 color atlas, an aged plate and so approximate, carries the same name [2]. Close neighbors are [[olive-green]], [[hunter-green]] and [[moss-green]], and it belongs to the family of [[green]] [2].

The books add no history of the name, so none is claimed here [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
This is a common painted color. It appears in 1,147 of the 23,781 paintings in our archive, 4.82 per cent, more often than 86 per cent of named colors, as photographed [3]. It peaks in the 1900s, at 5.5 per cent of paintings from then, 1.8 times the expected rate [3]. Inside a painting it is most often a hidden color, as in 45 per cent of 683 paintings, judged by lightness rank so varnish cannot fake it [3].

The most devoted painter is Edvard Weie, who uses it in 10 of the 33 works we hold, 5.1 times the baseline [3]. Paul Sérusier and Alfred Sisley also lean on it [3]. In Google Books the word peaks in the 1880s [4].
